issues.legal_issue: A civil court has jurisdiction over a suit for possession framed against alleged trespassers where the plaint, read as a whole, treats the defendants as trespassers after they deny the plaintiffs’ title and the alleged tenancy.
material_facts: The plaintiffs’ predecessor had purchased the disputed land and obtained a civil decree declaring his title.
The defendants had at one time paid rent, but later denied both the plaintiffs’ title and the tenancy in revenue proceedings.
The revenue authorities directed the plaintiffs to seek redress in the civil court.
The plaintiffs then sued for possession and mesne profits, treating the defendants as trespassers.
Although the plaint referred to an earlier tenancy, the suit was framed on the basis that the defendants had denied the plaintiffs’ title and tenancy.
issues.conclusion: The civil court had jurisdiction to try the suit. The bar under Sections 32 and 99 of the Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act did not prevent the civil court from hearing a suit framed against trespassers.
issues.legal_principle: The forum is determined by the allegations in the plaint read as a whole, not by the defence in the written statement. A suit against a trespasser lies in the civil court rather than the revenue court; the statutory provisions governing tenancy proceedings do not bar such a suit when it is not brought on the basis of a subsisting landlord-tenant relationship.

predicates.civil_suit_for_possession: The plaintiffs brought a civil proceeding seeking possession of land.
predicates.plaint_treats_defendants_as_trespassers: The plaintiffs’ pleading, read as a whole, treated the defendants as trespassers rather than seeking relief on the basis of a subsisting tenancy.
predicates.defendants_denied_title_and_tenancy: The defendants denied the plaintiffs’ title and the alleged tenancy.

issues.definition: When a civil suit seeks possession, the plaint treats the defendants as trespassers, and the defendants have denied title and tenancy, the civil court has jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A case cannot be finally resolved by accepting a lower appellate court’s findings on the merits when the High Court set aside the judgment solely on jurisdiction and did not examine the other issues.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court had decided the issues in favour of the plaintiffs.
The High Court set aside the judgment solely on the ground that the civil court lacked jurisdiction and did not decide the other issues.
The Supreme Court held that the civil court had jurisdiction, leaving the other issues for consideration.
issues.conclusion: The case was remanded to the High Court to decide the other issues on their merits; the lower appellate court’s findings were not to be confirmed without the High Court examining them.
issues.legal_principle: Where the High Court has decided a case only on jurisdiction and has not dealt with other issues, it is not fair to the opposing party to confirm the first appellate court’s findings on those issues without review by the High Court.

rule.if: appeal_from_high_court_judgment and high_court_decided_only_jurisdiction and other_issues_remain_undecided and lower_appellate_court_decided_merits

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_judgment: A party appealed from a High Court judgment.
predicates.high_court_decided_only_jurisdiction: The High Court disposed of the case solely on jurisdiction and did not decide the other issues.
predicates.other_issues_remain_undecided: Issues other than jurisdiction still require decision.
predicates.lower_appellate_court_decided_merits: A lower appellate court had decided the merits of the remaining issues.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a High Court judgment that decided only jurisdiction, other issues remain undecided, and a lower appellate court had decided those issues on the merits, the case is remanded for the High Court to review those issues.
